output:
I’ve been putting off writing this because I wanted to tell everyone properly, and then I let some of you hear it in bits and pieces instead. That was my fault. So here it is, all in one place.

The house in Glenmore, near Oughterard, is sold. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it will close on 15 January 2027.

I know some of you have already heard. Declan heard from Gráinne on WhatsApp, not from me, and he rang at two in the morning his time. He was very upset. He said I was “selling Dad”. I was hurt and angry, and I said things back that I shouldn’t have said. I’m sorry for the way you found out, and for the way I spoke to you, Declan. I should have told you myself, and I should have done it before the news travelled around the family. I’m not sorry for making the decision, but I am sorry I didn’t handle it better.

I don’t want anyone else hearing the closing date from someone else, so I’ll say it plainly: the house closes on 15 January 2027.

It is the old Mulkerrin place, built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig. Tom grew up there. We raised our family with that house as part of the background to everything, and there are memories in it that I can still walk into without warning. Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, naturally, and the cattle watched the whole thing. The children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan would refuse to come out until his lips were blue, and then argue that he wasn’t cold.

It has been a good house to us. That is true, and so is the fact that I can’t keep it going any longer.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I’ve driven out every fortnight to air the rooms and check the pipes. It’s about forty minutes each way. For a while, the routine gave me something to do. It kept me connected to the place and made it feel as if I was still looking after something that mattered to us both.

But a house can’t be kept up on memory alone. In September I had Ó Flaithearta’s survey done on the roof. The slates need work, as does the back chimney. Their quote was €38,000. There’s damp in the back bedroom too, and the septic tank needs replacing if I’m to sell to anyone. Those are only the immediate jobs. The house needs more of me than I have to give it.

Last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I was there for about twenty minutes before I could get myself up. I didn’t tell anyone until now. I suppose I didn’t want to worry you, and I didn’t want to admit how frightened I was. But I have been afraid of being alone in the house since then. I can’t keep pretending that a fall like that was nothing, or that I can carry on as before. I cannot keep maintaining the house.

I also wasn’t willing to wait until Declan’s summer visit to decide what to do. I know I should have consulted you before agreeing to the sale. I regret not doing that. At the same time, the house had been empty for long stretches, the work was piling up, and I was not able to keep going on the hope that we might all sort it out some day. Waiting would not have made the roof cheaper or the place easier to look after. I made the decision, and I understand that you may wish I had done it differently.

The couple buying the house are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. They have two small children, and Kevin is from Maam Cross. They want to live in the house, not turn it into a holiday let. That mattered to me. I could have taken a higher offer from the Dublin crowd who came in during the summer. I didn’t. The price the Joyces offered was fair, and I chose it on purpose. I wanted the house to be a home again, with children in it, rather than a place shut up most of the year.

Tom used to say that a house should have children in it, not be a museum. I’ve thought about that a lot over these last two years. At first, I couldn’t imagine letting the house go. It felt too close to letting go of Tom. But little by little I’ve come to realise that I can keep his memory without keeping the house. The memories are ours. They don’t belong to the walls, and they won’t disappear when the keys change hands.

I’m keeping the things that matter to us as a family: the dresser, which is going to Úna’s; Pádraig’s fiddle; the photographs; the Sacred Heart lamp; and the gate sign. Those will be looked after, and there’ll be time to decide where everything should go. If there’s something of yours in the house that I’ve missed, please tell me. I don’t want anyone to feel that a small thing was lost because I rushed past it.

Aoife and Kevin have said the family can come out and walk the land any time. I’m grateful to them for that. It’s kind of them, and I hope we’ll take them up on it.

Before the house is cleared, I’d love to have one last family day there. We’re planning it for Sunday, 13 December. If you can come, please do. We’ll have soup and sandwiches, and you should bring wellies. There’ll be time to walk around the house and the land, tell stories, and be together there without making it into a grand occasion. Just a family day, while we still can.

Declan, I know you’re reading this. I’m not angry with you. I understand why the news hurt, especially when it came from someone else, and I’m sorry I left you to hear it that way. I should have called you. I can’t undo that now, but I don’t want this to make a distance between us. The door is open. I’d like you to come in December if you can, and if you can’t, I still want us to talk.

I’m not asking anyone to agree with me straight away. I know the house means different things to each of us. I only want you to understand why I chose to sell it: the repairs, the driving, the worry of being there alone, and the fact that I can’t keep it up on my own. It was a difficult decision, but I made it because I believe it’s the right one for me now. And I believe Tom would have liked children to be running through those rooms again.

I love you all. I’m sorry this came to you badly. The sale is going ahead, and the closing date is 15 January 2027. If you can make it to Glenmore on Sunday, 13 December, I’ll put the soup on. Bring wellies.
